title: Psalm 66: Come and See What God Has Done
summary: All the earth is called to shout for joy and sing God's glory. The psalm recalls how God turned the sea into dry land, then how he tested and refined his people through fire and water before bringing them into abundance. In the last section one worshiper comes to the temple with offerings to pay his vows and tells everyone who fears God how God heard his prayer.
story: Psalm 66 continues the group of praise psalms (65 to 68) that follow the long run of laments in Book II. It is the first psalm since Psalm 50 without David's name in its heading. It widens the circle of praise: Psalm 65 celebrated God as the hope of the ends of the earth, and Psalm 66 calls the whole earth to shout to him. Its most striking feature is its movement from the community to the individual. The first half speaks for Israel as a nation, recalling the exodus and a time of hard testing, and the second half is the testimony of one person who made vows in distress and now comes to keep them.
historical:
The heading names no author and gives no occasion. The psalm's reference to the people being tested, laid under burdens, and ridden over by men, followed by deliverance into abundance, suggests a national crisis that ended in rescue. Some interpreters have connected it with Jerusalem's deliverance from the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC, when Hezekiah prayed and the city was spared (2 Kings 18 to 19; Isaiah 36 to 37). Others think of the return from exile after 538 BC. Still others think the psalm was written for regular use at the temple, where individuals came to pay vows and the community remembered God's acts. The text doesn't settle the question.

The second half assumes the sacrificial system of the temple in Jerusalem. The worshiper brings burnt offerings of fatlings, rams, bulls, and goats, a lavish offering, perhaps suggesting someone of means or a representative figure such as a king or leader speaking for the nation. Some scholars think the “I” of the second half is the king; others take it as any grateful worshiper.
cultural:
Verse 6 recalls two water crossings: the sea turned into dry land, the Red Sea at the exodus (Exodus 14), and passing through the waters on foot, which may also allude to the crossing of the Jordan under Joshua (Joshua 3). The Hebrew word in the second line is river, which fits the Jordan. Israel told these stories at its festivals, and the psalm invites everyone to come and see as if they were present.

Verse 10 uses the image of refining silver. Metalworkers heated silver ore in a furnace until the impurities (the dross) separated and could be removed, sometimes repeating the process several times (Proverbs 17:3; Malachi 3:3). The net, the burdens on the back, and people riding over their heads are images of capture, forced labor, and humiliation in war. The burnt offering, in which the whole animal was burned on the altar, was the offering of complete dedication. Paying vows publicly was part of Israel's worship: the person told the gathered worshipers what God had done (Psalm 22:25; 116:14, 18).
literary: The psalm moves from the widest circle to the narrowest. Verses 1 to 4 call all the earth to praise. Verses 5 to 7 invite people to come and see God's works, recalling the exodus. Verses 8 to 12 call the peoples to bless God and recount Israel's testing. Verses 13 to 15 switch to the first person singular, as one worshiper brings offerings. Verses 16 to 20 invite all who fear God to come and hear what God has done for him. The two invitations, come and see (verse 5) and come and listen (verse 16), mark the two halves: God's works for the nation and God's work for one person. Selah appears three times, marking pauses after the calls to praise and the offerings.

outline.t: All the earth called to praise
Come and see: the sea turned to dry land
Tested and refined, brought into abundance
Come and listen: God heard my prayer

doctrines.note: The people's trials are described as God's testing and refining. Suffering is not presented as meaningless or outside God's control but as a furnace that purifies, and it ends in abundance.

Verse 18 says that if the worshiper had cherished iniquity in his heart, the Lord would not have listened. Prayer is not a technique but a relationship, and it cannot coexist with sin that is held on to rather than confessed.
The psalm calls all the earth and all peoples to praise and invites all who fear God to hear one person's testimony. Israel's story and each worshiper's story are meant to be told to the world.

words.note: Tsaraph, to refine or smelt. Verse 10 says God has refined his people like silver. The word is used of metalworkers purifying precious metals and, in the prophets, of God purifying his people through trial (Isaiah 48:10; Zechariah 13:9).

Bachan, to test or examine. It is paired with refining in verse 10. The testing is not to discover something God doesn't know but to prove and purify what is there. The word is also used of God testing hearts and minds (Psalm 7:9; Jeremiah 17:10).

Neder, vow. The worshiper comes to fulfill vows his lips promised in distress (verses 13 and 14). Keeping a vow was an act of integrity and gratitude, and Scripture warns against making vows lightly or failing to keep them (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5).
Chesed, loving devotion. The psalm ends by blessing God, who has not withheld his loving devotion. After all the testing and trials, the final word is God's steadfast covenant love.

christ: The psalm's call for all the earth to worship God anticipates the New Testament's vision of every nation praising God through Christ (Revelation 5:9; 7:9-10). The image of refining through fire is taken up in 1 Peter 1:6-7, where the trials of believers are said to prove the genuineness of their faith, more precious than gold refined by fire. The exodus and the crossing of waters are read in the New Testament as patterns of salvation and baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1-2). And the testimony of verse 16, come and listen, and I will declare what He has done, echoes the witness of the first disciples, who could not stop speaking about what they had seen and heard (Acts 4:20). These are thematic connections; the New Testament does not quote Psalm 66 directly.

hard.q: Does verse 18 mean that God won't hear the prayers of people who sin?
hard.a: Verse 18 says, “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.” Read alone, it could suggest that only the sinless can pray, which would leave no one able to pray at all. The verb means to regard or look at with favor, and the line describes someone holding on to sin, treasuring it and refusing to turn from it, while asking God for help. Other passages make the same point (Isaiah 1:15; 59:2; Proverbs 28:9). The psalm itself is not the prayer of a sinless person; it is the testimony of someone who came to God honestly. The whole Bible holds out God's readiness to hear the prayer of a repentant sinner (Psalm 51; Luke 18:13-14). The warning is against hypocrisy, not against imperfection.

questions: The psalm invites people to come and see what God has done. What has God done in your life that you could invite others to see?
Verse 10 says God refines his people like silver. How have hard times refined you?
Verse 18 warns against cherishing iniquity in the heart. Is there anything you are holding on to that is hindering your prayers?
